title: Шаблон 3
description: Hot Take для подростков: спорный пост, групповой чат, грамматика из чата, Sentence Builder, дебаты с учителем и ответ на пост.

stages.title: Warm Up
stages.subtitle: Hot Take
stages.instructions:
This is a five-minute Warm-Up: the learner reads a short provocative social-media post, a “hot take”, and says whether they agree.
Keep everything directly connected to the Warm-Up topic. Image prompts must be in English.

component.text:
**Goal:** Get the student talking from the first minute. The post is a “hot take”: a strong, slightly provocative opinion. There is no right answer, only good reasons.

**Say:** “Look at this post. Do you agree or disagree with it? Why?”

**Teacher's Tips:**

- **Take the other side:** Whatever the student says, gently argue the opposite: “Really? But some people say…” This prepares them for the debate later in the lesson.
- **Push for reasons:** If the answer is just “Yes” or “No”, point to the Speaking Support box and ask: “Can you say why?”
- **Fluency first:** Do not correct grammar now. Note one or two mistakes for the end of the lesson.

post.rule:
A short social-media post by a teenage blogger with one strong, slightly provocative but harmless opinion about the Warm-Up topic: a “hot take” that teenagers will want to argue with.
Start with the blogger’s handle in bold, like **@name**, then write two or three short sentences in natural English at the target CEFR level. You may add one or two emojis and one hashtag. No other Markdown.
post.example: **@maxi_talks** 🔥 Hot take: phones should stay at home on school days. We spend the whole evening on our screens anyway. Who’s with me? #NoPhoneZone

avatarImagePrompt.rule: An image prompt for a small circular avatar of the blogger who wrote the post. A modern educational illustration suitable for teenagers, with no text. Avoid childish or preschool aesthetics.
avatarImagePrompt.example: Small circular avatar of a confident teenage blogger with headphones around the neck, bright flat colours, modern educational illustration, no text.

chrome.title: What’s Your Take?
chrome.instruction: Answer the questions out loud. Give a reason for every answer.

blocks.instructions: hotTakeQuestions ask what the learner thinks about the post and connect it to their own life. The first question asks whether they agree with the post.

questions.question: Do you agree with the post? Why or why not?
questions.followUp: What would your best friend say?

questions.question: How often do you use your phone at school?
questions.followUp: What do you use it for?

questions.question: Can a phone help you learn something?

component.title: Speaking Support
component.text:
I totally agree because…

No way! I think…

It depends. On the one hand… On the other hand…

stages.title: Target Vocabulary
stages.subtitle: Unlock the Words
stages.instructions:
This is an eight-minute Target Vocabulary stage: the learner meets the words of the lesson, matches them with pictures, recalls them from Russian hints and plays a guessing game.
All English must be natural, at the target CEFR level and directly connected to the lesson topic.
Whenever a field refers to a vocabulary term, copy it exactly, including spelling, capitalization, articles, and “to”.

component.text:
**Task 1:** say “Here are the words we need to argue about our topic. Match them with the pictures. Start with the words you know.” After matching, read the Vocabulary card together and check the meanings.

**Task 2:** say “Read each sentence and type the English word for the Russian hint.” Ask the student to read the whole sentence aloud.

**Task 3:** say “Let’s play! Choose a word and describe it without saying it. I’ll guess. Then it’s my turn.” Go first to show how it works.

**Pronunciation:** Check tricky words in the Cambridge or Oxford Learner’s dictionaries, play the audio and ask the student to repeat.

blocks.instructions: vocabularyItems: words or short phrases teenagers need to give opinions and argue about the topic.

items.definition: an official rule that says people must not do something
something that takes your attention away from what you are doing
the time you spend looking at a phone, tablet or computer
set so that it makes no sound
a sudden dangerous situation when you need help quickly
an online conversation between several people
a small cupboard where you can lock your phone away
look at your phone to see if someone wrote to you

chrome.title: Task 1 · Match the Words
chrome.instruction: Match the words with the pictures.

blocks.instructions:
Use every term of vocabularyItems, copied exactly, in the same order.
The pictures appear together, so each one must make its term recognizable and clearly distinguishable from every other term in the set.
Plan all image concepts together before writing the final prompts. Give each term a distinct visual scene with a clear identifying cue. Compare each scene against all other terms: if another term would be an equally reasonable answer, redesign the scene.
Avoid similar scenes for different terms. Prefer concrete actions, objects, and observable contrasts over facial expressions, mood, or generic topic-related settings.
For abstract terms, use a simple two-panel scene if needed to show a change or a contrast. Specify what appears in each panel.
Write each imagePrompt as a self-contained drawing instruction: the main subject, exact action, and identifying visual cue first, then style and background. Make the cue large enough to recognize in a small thumbnail and do not rely on readable words, labels, or numbers.
Use a consistent modern educational illustration style across the set.

items.imagePrompt: A big red crossed-out circle over a smartphone lying on a school desk, square modern educational illustration, no text.
Two-panel scene: a teenager writing in a notebook; then the same teenager looking away at a buzzing phone with the pen stopped. Square modern educational illustration, no text.
A teenager on a sofa staring at a glowing phone while the window behind changes from day to night, square modern educational illustration, no text.
Close-up of a thumb pressing the side switch of a smartphone, a crossed-out speaker symbol on the screen, square modern educational illustration, no text.
A worried teenager making a phone call next to a friend who has fallen off a bike, square modern educational illustration, no text.
A phone screen full of colourful chat bubbles from five different small round avatars, square modern educational illustration, no text.
A student putting a phone into one of many small metal lockers on a school corridor wall and turning a key, square modern educational illustration, no text.
A teenager quickly pulling a phone out of a pocket to look at a new notification, square modern educational illustration, no text.

chrome.title: Task 3 · Describe and Guess
chrome.instruction: Take turns with your teacher. Describe the word without saying it. Can your partner guess it?

blocks.instructions: Every item of describeAndGuessTerms is a term of vocabularyItems, copied exactly; use different terms.

stages.title: Group Chat
stages.subtitle: Read the Class Chat
stages.instructions:
This is a seven-minute reading stage. The reading text is a class group chat: three or four teenagers argue about the lesson topic and agree on something at the end.
The supplied Grammar topic is authoritative: use exactly that grammar in the chat, because the Grammar Presentation later takes its examples from it.
All content must be natural English at the target CEFR level. Make distractors plausible but clearly wrong.

component.text:
**Before reading:** say “Our class has a group chat too! Let’s read what these friends think about our topic.” Ask the student to guess from the title what the friends argue about.

**Task 1:** Read the chat together. Weaker students read it aloud; stronger students read silently first. Ask the student to find the message that proves each answer.

**Task 2:** Ask the questions and react like a friend in the chat: “Really? Why?”

**Keep in mind:** The chat is full of the grammar of the next stage. Don’t explain it yet.

blocks.instructions:
Select 4 to 6 distinct entries from the supplied Target Vocabulary and include each of them exactly and naturally in the chat.
Write the text as a group chat. Every paragraph is one message in the form **Name:** message, short and informal like real teenagers write; one or two emojis in the whole chat are fine.
The friends start with different opinions, give reasons, and agree on something at the end.
Include 5 to 7 clear and accurate examples of the target grammar in different messages, without explaining the grammar.
title is the name of the chat; subtitle is the question the friends argue about.
headerImagePrompt describes a group avatar for the chat; textImagePrompt describes a scene connected to the argument.

example.title: Class 8B 💬
example.subtitle: Should our school ban phones?
example.text:
**Mia:** Did you see the news? From Monday our school wants a phone ban! 😱

**Leo:** Honestly, I think it’s a good idea. Phones are a huge distraction in class. We shouldn’t check messages every five minutes.

**Mia:** But what about an emergency? I should be able to call my mum.

**Sara:** You can use the phone in the office. And we could put our phones in a phone locker in the morning.

**Leo:** Exactly. Teachers should keep the rules simple.

**Tom:** I don’t agree. We use phones for homework and for our group chat. The school shouldn’t take them away completely.

**Sara:** Maybe students should keep them on silent and use them only in the break?

**Mia:** That sounds fair. We should talk to the head teacher about it! 👍

**Tom:** Deal. And less screen time at lunch, I promise 😂
example.headerImagePrompt: Small round group avatar with four smiling teenagers' faces, bright flat colours, modern educational illustration, no text.
example.textImagePrompt: Wide scene of four teenagers arguing in a friendly way at a school table, one holding up a phone, modern educational illustration, no text.

chrome.title: Task 1. Who Thinks What?
chrome.instruction: Read the chat and choose the correct answer.

blocks.instructions: chatQuestions ask who said what, why the friends think so, and what they agree on at the end. Every answer is stated in the chat.

questions.question: Who thinks phones are a distraction in class?
questions.explanation: Leo says phones are a huge distraction in class.

questions.question: Why is Mia worried about the ban?
options: She wants to call her mum in an emergency.
She wants to play games in the break.
She needs her phone for a test.
questions.answer: She wants to call her mum in an emergency.
questions.explanation: Mia says she should be able to call her mum in an emergency.

questions.question: What does Sara suggest?
options: Keeping phones on silent and using them only in the break
questions.answer: Keeping phones on silent and using them only in the break
questions.explanation: Sara says students should keep them on silent and use them only in the break.

questions.question: What do the friends decide to do?
questions.explanation: Mia says they should talk to the head teacher, and Tom agrees.

chrome.title: Task 2 · Whose Side Are You On?
chrome.instruction: Answer the questions out loud. There are no right or wrong answers!

blocks.instructions: sideQuestions ask whose opinion in the chat the learner shares and connect the argument to the learner’s own life.

questions.question: Whose idea in the chat do you like most?
Do you use your phone during the school day?
Is a phone ban fair for students your age?

stages.title: Grammar Presentation
stages.subtitle: Spot It in the Chat
stages.instructions:
This is a five-minute Grammar Presentation built on guided discovery: the learner finds the target grammar in the group chat they have just read, completes the rule and checks it.
The supplied Grammar topic is authoritative: present exactly that grammar.
Where a slot asks for it, take examples from the supplied Group chat; elsewhere use the lesson topic as the context.
All copy must be natural English at the target CEFR level.

component.text:
**Guided discovery:** Don’t explain the rule first. Let the student notice it in the chat they have just read.

**Say:** “Do you remember the group chat? Here are five messages from it. Look at the words in bold. What do they have in common?”

**Then:** Work through the questions, let the student complete the rule and confirm it with Quick Rule.

**Check:** In the last task, ask the student to explain each choice and to correct the wrong sentences aloud.

chatExamples.rule: Exactly five sentences from the supplied Group chat that use the target grammar, copied exactly, as a Markdown numbered list (1. to 5.), one per line. End each line with “ — ” and the speaker’s name in italics. In every sentence, wrap the target grammar form in exactly one pair of **bold** Markdown markers. No heading or introduction.
chatExamples.example:
1. We **shouldn’t check** messages every five minutes. — *Leo*
2. I **should be** able to call my mum. — *Mia*
3. Teachers **should keep** the rules simple. — *Leo*
4. The school **shouldn’t take** them away completely. — *Tom*
5. We **should talk** to the head teacher about it! — *Mia*

conceptCheckingQuestions.rule: Exactly four concept-checking questions about the chat sentences as a Markdown numbered list (1. to 4.), one question per line. Keep them concise and guide the learner to discover meaning, use, and form. No heading or introduction.
conceptCheckingQuestions.example:
1. In sentence 3, is Leo giving advice or talking about the past?
2. Which word means “it’s a bad idea”: should or shouldn’t?
3. What comes after should: check, to check or checks?
4. Does should change after he, she or it?

chrome.title: Complete the Rule
chrome.instruction: Drag the correct words into the gaps.

blocks.instructions: Together, ruleSentences state the grammar rule of the lesson: each sentence is one clear rule statement, and its gap is a key word or short phrase of the rule.

sentences: We use should to give [[advice]] or to say that something is a good idea.
We use [[shouldn’t]] to say that something is a bad idea.
After should we use the [[base form]] of the verb: should keep, not should to keep.
Should is the [[same]] for all persons: I should, she should, they should.

blocks.instructions: Use concise Markdown bullet points to cover meaning, affirmative form, and relevant negative/question forms, with an example from the lesson topic where useful.

sections.title: SHOULD
sections.text:
- **meaning:** advice, a good idea
- **form:** should + base verb
- **example:** “You should put your phone on silent.”

sections.title: SHOULDN’T
sections.text:
- **meaning:** a bad idea
- **form:** shouldn’t + base verb
- **example:** “We shouldn’t check messages in class.”

sections.title: QUESTIONS
sections.text:
- **form:** Should + subject + base verb?
- **example:** “Should we ban phones?”
- **short answers:** Yes, we should. / No, we shouldn’t.

chrome.title: Check the Rule. Tick the correct sentences.
chrome.instruction: Read the sentences and tick the grammatically correct ones.

blocks.instructions:
One question: "Which three sentences are grammatically correct?"
The options are six sentences that check the grammar rule of the lesson. Exactly three are grammatically correct; each of the other three has one clear, typical error in the target grammar. The answers are the three correct sentences.
explanation: start with the line "Incorrect sentences:", then a numbered Markdown list, one item per incorrect sentence in any order: the sentence in italics — what is wrong and the corrected sentence. Example item: *He shoulds ask his teacher first.* — Should doesn’t change: He should ask his teacher first.
Do not use Markdown in the question or options.

questions.question: Which three sentences are grammatically correct?
options: You should keep your phone in your bag.
He shoulds ask his teacher first.
Students shouldn’t use phones in tests.
We should to put our phones on silent.
Should we talk to the head teacher?
You don’t should check messages in class.
answers: You should keep your phone in your bag.
Students shouldn’t use phones in tests.
Should we talk to the head teacher?
questions.explanation:
Incorrect sentences:
1. *He shoulds ask his teacher first.* — Should doesn’t change: He should ask his teacher first.
2. *We should to put our phones on silent.* — Use the base form after should: We should put our phones on silent.
3. *You don’t should check messages in class.* — The negative is shouldn’t: You shouldn’t check messages in class.

stages.title: Grammar Focus
stages.subtitle: Build & Fix
stages.instructions:
This is an eight-minute Grammar Focus with three controlled-practice tasks written as chat messages: build messages from word cards, fix messages that autocorrect broke, and complete messages with the right form.
The supplied Grammar topic is authoritative: every task practises exactly that grammar accurately.
Use the lesson topic as one coherent context and reuse some supplied Target Vocabulary where it fits.
All content must be natural English at the target CEFR level. Do not use Markdown or HTML, except the bold numbers of gapMessages.

component.text:
**Task 1:** say “These chat messages fell apart! Put the cards in the right order.” Let the student use the hints if they get stuck, then ask them to read each message aloud.

**Task 2:** say “Autocorrect broke these messages. There is one mistake in each. Can you fix it?” Ask the student to explain the rule behind each correction.

**Task 3:** say “Complete the messages with the correct form of the words in brackets.”

**Correct now:** mistakes in the target grammar. **Leave for later:** small slips that do not stop communication.

chrome.title: Task 1. Build the Message
chrome.instruction: Put the cards in the right order to make a chat message.

blocks.instructions: builderItems are short chat messages about the lesson topic; each uses the target grammar.

items.sentence: We should [put our phones] [on silent] in class.
Should we [use our phones] for homework?
You should [call your parents] in an emergency.
We should [turn off] [our phones] and [our tablets] in tests.
otherOrders: We should [turn off] [our tablets] and [our phones] in tests.

chrome.title: Task 2. Autocorrect Fail! Fix the Messages.
chrome.instruction: There is one mistake in each message. Rewrite it correctly.

blocks.instructions: correctionItems are short chat messages about the lesson topic.

items.incorrect: You should to put your phone in the locker.
corrections: You should put your phone in the locker.

items.incorrect: Students shouldn’t uses phones in tests.
corrections: Students shouldn’t use phones in tests.

items.incorrect: Do we should switch off our phones?
corrections: Should we switch off our phones?

items.incorrect: She shoulds ask the teacher first.
corrections: She should ask the teacher first.

items.incorrect: We don’t should check messages in class.
corrections: We shouldn’t check messages in class.
We should not check messages in class.

items.incorrect: Should I calling my mum in an emergency?
corrections: Should I call my mum in an emergency?

chrome.title: Task 3. Complete the Messages.
chrome.instruction: Type the correct form of the words in brackets.

blocks.instructions:
gapMessages is a numbered list of six separate short chat messages about the lesson topic, one per line, each starting with its number in bold (**1.**) and with exactly one gap.
Each gap tests a form of the grammar of the lesson; each cue gives the words the learner must change, for example “not play” or “we / use”.

example.text:
**1.** Students [[1]] games during lessons.
**2.** You [[2]] your phone on silent in class.
**3.** [[3]] our phones for the project?
**4.** I think teachers [[4]] our phones away.
**5.** We [[5]] to each other at lunch.
**6.** Parents [[6]] their children during lessons.

stages.title: Debate
stages.subtitle: Agree or Disagree?
stages.instructions:
This is a ten-minute debate between the learner and the teacher about one clear question on the lesson topic. Each side has a secret role card; in the end they must agree on one fair solution.
All content must be natural English at the target CEFR level. Do not use Russian or HTML, and use Markdown only where a rule asks for it.
Do not turn the debate into a grammar exercise.

component.text:
**Set up:** Read How to Debate together. The student argues for one side, you argue for the other. Keep your card secret.

**Say:** “Let’s have a debate! Read your card. You have one minute to think of your reasons.”

**During the debate:** Disagree politely and ask for reasons: “Why do you think so?” Use the Speaking Support phrases yourself so the student hears them.

**If the student gets stuck:** Point to one phrase in Speaking Support or offer a choice of two ideas.

**Finish:** Agree on one solution together. Show the Example Debate if the student needs a model.

**Correct:** only when the meaning is unclear. Note other mistakes for later.

component.title: How to Debate
steps: Read your card. Keep it secret.
Say what you think and give two reasons.
Listen to your partner and react. Agree or disagree politely.
Agree on one fair solution together.

blocks.instructions:
Select 3 to 4 distinct entries from the supplied Target Vocabulary and use each of them exactly and naturally in the role cards and the Example Debate.
The two roles take opposite sides of one debate question about the lesson topic: Student argues for one side, Teacher for the other.
want: the two main arguments of that side; avoid: what that side does not want to happen; secret: two private facts that help that side; mission: two short actions, the first of them is to use three words from the lesson.
The student and teacher goal strings must be exactly the same: agree on one fair solution together.

want: Keep your phone for an emergency
secret: Your bus is often late, so you text your mum
The class group chat has all the homework
mission: Use three words from the lesson
student.goal: Agree on one fair phone rule for our school.

secret: Last week three phones rang in a test
Many students want less screen time
mission: Use three words from the lesson
teacher.goal: Agree on one fair phone rule for our school.

blocks.instructions: Make the phrases suitable for a polite debate about the topic. Keep clarification phrases generally reusable.

exampleDebate.rule: An Example Debate of 6 to 8 turns in which Teacher and Student speak in turn. Start every turn with **Teacher:** or **Student:**, put an empty line between turns and write it in English only. It is a short polite debate that follows the role cards, uses phrases like those in Speaking Support and ends with the shared solution.
exampleDebate.example:
**Teacher:** I think phones should stay in a phone locker during lessons. They are a big distraction.

**Student:** I see your point, but what about an emergency? I should be able to call my mum.

**Teacher:** That’s fair. But students shouldn’t check messages in class.

**Student:** OK. What if we keep our phones on silent in our bags?

**Teacher:** Good idea. And no phones at lunch, so we have less screen time.

**Student:** Deal! So we agree: phones on silent in bags, and we only use them in an emergency.

stages.title: Create
stages.subtitle: Reply to the Post
stages.instructions:
This is a five-minute writing stage: the learner writes a reply to the hot-take post from the Warm-Up, using the target grammar and words of the lesson.
All content must be natural English at the target CEFR level.

component.text:
**Say:** “Remember the hot take from the start of the lesson? Now you are an expert! Write your reply to the post.”

**Support:** Weaker students can start from the model sentence and write three sentences. Stronger students add a question to the blogger at the end.

**After writing:** Ask the student to read the reply aloud like a real post. Praise one strong argument, then correct one or two mistakes together.

chrome.title: Your Reply
chrome.instruction: Write your reply to the post in 4–6 sentences. Your answer will be checked by the teacher.

blocks.instructions:
replyTask.prompt asks the learner to reply to the hot-take post from the Warm-Up without quoting the post or naming its author: one short opening line, a blank line, then exactly four Markdown bullet points in this order: say if you agree or disagree; give two reasons; one instruction to use the target grammar with the key form in **bold**; use words from the lesson.
replyTask.imagePrompt shows a teenager typing a reply under a social-media post on a smartphone.

situation.prompt:
Remember the hot take about phones at school? Now it’s your turn to reply.

- Say if you agree or disagree.
- Give two reasons.
- Give one piece of advice with **should** or **shouldn’t**.
- Use words from the lesson.
situation.imagePrompt: A teenager on a school bench typing a reply under a social-media post on a smartphone, heart and comment icons floating around the phone, modern educational illustration for teenagers, bright flat colours, no text.

component.title: Support

replyWords.rule: Exactly six distinct entries from Target Vocabulary, each copied exactly, separated by commas on one line. No Markdown, no full stop.
replyWords.example: ban, distraction, emergency, on silent, screen time, phone locker

modelSentence.rule: One natural sentence of a reply to the post that uses the target grammar, without quotation marks.
modelSentence.example: I don’t agree with a phone ban, but we should keep our phones on silent in class.

stages.title: Wrap-Up
stages.subtitle: How Did It Go?
stages.instructions:
This is a two-minute Wrap-Up: the learner rates the lesson and hears that the homework comes in the next stage.
All copy must be natural English at the target CEFR level.

component.text:
**Say:** “Great debate today! How do you feel about the lesson? Choose an answer for each line.”

**Then:** Tell the student that the homework is in the next stage. Open it together, read the task and show where to write and how to hand it in.

**Positive ending:** Praise one good argument the student made in the debate.

component.title: Self-assessment: How do you feel about today’s lesson?
Coming Up: Homework
component.text: Your homework is in the next stage. You will write a short comment for your class group chat and hand it in. Your teacher will check it and give you feedback.

stages.title: Homework
stages.subtitle: Post Your Comment
stages.instructions:
This is the homework stage, done after the lesson: the learner writes a comment for the class group chat that reviews the lesson topic, grammar and words, and hands it in; the teacher grades it later.
All copy must be natural English at the target CEFR level.

component.text:
**In class:** Read the task together and check that the student understands the question. Show the word counter and the **Hand in** button.

**After the lesson:** The student writes at home and hands the comment in. Open this stage, read the comment, give 1–5 stars and write one thing that is good and one thing to fix.

**Needs changes:** If the comment is off-topic or has no target grammar, return it with a short note instead of a grade.

component.title: Post Your Comment
component.instruction: Write your comment, then hand it in. Your teacher will check it.

homeworkTask.rule: A short homework task for the learner: write a comment of 50–70 words for the class group chat about a question on the lesson topic, using the target grammar at least three times and three words from the Target Vocabulary. Name the grammar form in **bold**. Two short paragraphs separated by a blank line; no heading or list.
homeworkTask.example:
Write a comment of 50–70 words for your class group chat: *Should our school ban phones?*

Use **should** or **shouldn’t** at least three times and three words from today’s lesson.

homeworkWords.rule: Exactly six distinct entries from Target Vocabulary, each copied exactly, separated by commas on one line. No Markdown, no full stop.
homeworkWords.example: ban, emergency, distraction, screen time, check messages, group chat

homeworkStarter.rule: The opening sentence of a group-chat comment that answers the homework question and uses the target grammar, without quotation marks.
homeworkStarter.example: I think our school shouldn’t ban phones, but we should use them only at break.
